_meta.schema: tree: id, world, title, symptom; nodes keyed by id — each: q (question) + options [{label, next}] OR answer {diagnosis, fix, lesson}. Entry node is always 'start'.

trees.title: It hangs and nothing happens
trees.symptom: A play or ad-hoc command sits there with no output and no error.

start.q: Re-run the exact command with -vvv. What is the last line before the hang? (It's usually in the last 3 lines of output — look for the word ESTABLISH.)

options.label: It hangs before any connection line

ssh.q: Run the printed ssh command yourself (copy it from the -vvv output). What happens?

options.label: It prompts to accept a host key

answer.diagnosis: Key auth isn't working for the user Ansible connects as, so SSH falls back to an invisible password prompt.
answer.fix: Check ansible-inventory --host <host> for ansible_user; test ssh <user>@<host> by hand; fix authorized_keys (mode 600, right user, restorecon -Rv ~/.ssh). Short-term: -k to prompt for the SSH password.
answer.lesson: A hang in a batch tool is almost always an invisible interactive prompt.

answer.diagnosis: First contact with this host — sshd wants the host key accepted and there's no terminal to say yes.
answer.fix: SSH to the host once by hand and accept (verify the fingerprint), or pre-populate known_hosts for the fleet. If the key CHANGED on a host that wasn't rebuilt, stop and treat it as a security event.
answer.lesson: Pre-populate known_hosts as part of provisioning; never blanket-disable host key checking to make a symptom go away.

answer.diagnosis: Transport-level: firewall silently dropping (no reject), wrong IP, or the host is wedged.
answer.fix: ping it; check ansible_host in inventory; from console check sshd and firewall-cmd --list-services. A DROP rule (vs REJECT) produces exactly this silent hang.
answer.lesson: Silent hang at connect = packets going into a black hole. REJECT fails fast; DROP wastes your afternoon.

answer.diagnosis: The hang is on the control node itself — a local/delegated task waiting on something: usually sudo wanting a password (become without -K), or the task genuinely running long.
answer.fix: If the task uses become: re-run with -K or fix sudoers for your user. Otherwise ps on the control node to see what the forked task is doing.
answer.lesson: delegate_to: localhost + become still needs a sudo password — the prompt is just as invisible locally as remotely.

answer.diagnosis: Module staging to the remote temp directory is wedged — slow/broken sftp, or remote filesystem issues.
answer.fix: Check disk space and the remote_tmp path on the target; try pipelining=true (bypasses staging) as a TEST to confirm the diagnosis, then fix the underlying temp-dir problem.
answer.lesson: Pipelining proving the workaround works is evidence, not a fix. Cure the temp dir.

answer.diagnosis: Ansible is stuck before connecting: usually a dynamic inventory script hanging, or a vars_prompt waiting for input you can't see.
answer.fix: Run ansible-inventory --list by itself — if it hangs, the inventory source is the problem. Check for vars_prompt in the play.
answer.lesson: Everything before ESTABLISH CONNECTION is control-node-side: inventory, vars, plugins.

trees.title: UNREACHABLE / connection refused
trees.symptom: Hosts report UNREACHABLE!, connection refused, or auth failures.

start.q: Can you ssh to the target BY HAND as the same user Ansible uses? (Check the user with ansible-inventory --host <host>.)

manualok.q: Then Ansible is connecting differently than you are. Compare ansible-inventory --host <host> to your manual command. Any mismatch in user, port, key, or host?

answer.diagnosis: Inventory vars point Ansible at a different door than the one you tested.
answer.fix: Correct ansible_user / ansible_port / ansible_host (or the group_vars they inherit from). Re-test with ansible <host> -m ping.
answer.lesson: Debug the connection Ansible makes, not the one you make. ansible-inventory --host is the truth.

answer.diagnosis: Extra SSH arguments (ssh_common_args, ProxyJump, control persistence) or an ssh_connection config difference is in play.
answer.fix: ansible-config dump --only-changed | grep -i ssh; run with -vvv and execute its exact ssh line by hand.
answer.lesson: The -vvv output contains the literal ssh command — run it yourself and the mystery usually confesses.

answer.diagnosis: Authentication is genuinely broken for that user: key missing, wrong permissions, or password auth disabled.
answer.fix: On the target: authorized_keys present for that user, chmod 600, home dir not group-writable, restorecon -Rv ~/.ssh. Check /var/log/secure on the target — sshd logs WHY it refused.
answer.lesson: sshd tells you the reason in /var/log/secure; read the server's side of the story, not just the client's.

answer.diagnosis: Network path or sshd availability problem — nothing Ansible can do until transport exists.
answer.fix: ping; check VLAN/firewall path; from console: systemctl status sshd, ss -tlnp | grep :22, firewall-cmd --list-services.
answer.lesson: UNREACHABLE is never an Ansible bug. Fix the road before blaming the truck.

trees.title: Connects fine, but modules fail (raw works, ping doesn't)
trees.symptom: SSH works, raw commands work, but real modules error or fail to run.

start.q: Run: ansible <host> -m ping. What does the error mention?

answer.diagnosis: Module staging directory (remote_tmp, default ~/.ansible/tmp) can't be created or used: broken home, full disk, noexec mount, or perms.
answer.fix: As the ansible user on the target: mkdir -p ~/.ansible/tmp; df -h; mount | grep -E 'noexec.*(home|tmp)'. Fix the filesystem condition, or point remote_tmp somewhere sane. Pipelining=true masks this — fine as a speed setting, wrong as a fix.
answer.lesson: Scar #002: we shipped the workaround and left the disease. Verify the cure, not the silence.

answer.diagnosis: The target lacks Python where Ansible expects it — modules are Python programs that run ON the target.
answer.fix: ansible <host> -m raw -a 'ls /usr/bin/python*'; set ansible_python_interpreter accordingly, or install python3 via -m raw on minimal images.
answer.lesson: raw and script are the only modules that don't need Python — that's why they're the probes.

answer.diagnosis: sudoers requiretty (legacy hardening) rejects Ansible's TTY-less sudo — and conflicts with pipelining.
answer.fix: sudoers.d drop-in: 'Defaults:<ansible_user> !requiretty'; validate with visudo -c.
answer.lesson: requiretty + pipelining is a known bad pair; exempt the automation user explicitly.

answer.diagnosis: The module itself is failing — arguments, missing packages, or target-side state.
answer.fix: Read the module's msg field (run with -vvv for the full JSON). ansible-doc <module> for required args and notes. Reproduce the operation by hand on the target.
answer.lesson: Module errors return structured JSON — the msg field is usually the whole answer, unabbreviated.

trees.title: Worked Friday, broken Monday
trees.symptom: Nothing 'changed', but the same playbook now fails.

start.q: Something changed — the job is finding it. Where did you run it from, and is it the SAME directory/user as Friday?

answer.diagnosis: Config discovery changed: a different ansible.cfg won (precedence: $ANSIBLE_CONFIG, ./ansible.cfg, ~/.ansible.cfg, /etc/ansible/ansible.cfg) — different inventory, different connection settings.
answer.fix: ansible --version (look at 'config file ='); ansible-config dump --only-changed. Also check for the world-writable-directory warning that silently disables ./ansible.cfg.
answer.lesson: Scar #001 territory: moving where you run from moves which config wins.

what.q: Diff the environment: git log on the repo since Friday; dnf history on control node AND targets; any password/cert/key expirations?

answer.diagnosis: The playbook/inventory content changed under you.
answer.fix: git diff <friday>..HEAD — read every changed line of inventory and group_vars first; that's where blast-radius bugs live.
answer.lesson: Source of truth in git means git log IS your change log. Read it before debugging anything else.

answer.diagnosis: An update moved the ground: new ansible-core deprecations, new openssh defaults, new python.
answer.fix: dnf history info <id> on the relevant box; check ansible --version vs what Friday used; read deprecation warnings in the output — they name the change.
answer.lesson: Pin automation-critical package versions, or at least subscribe your eyeballs to dnf history.

answer.diagnosis: Likely an inventory/vars drift or an expired external dependency (cert, token, password rotation).
answer.fix: ansible-inventory --host <failing-host> and compare to a working host; check age of vault-stored credentials; run the failing task alone with -vvv.
answer.lesson: When 'nothing changed', something expired. Time is a change agent too.

trees.title: It ran green but did nothing
trees.symptom: Play recap all ok/green, yet the change isn't on the targets.

start.q: In the recap, did the tasks report ok= or changed= for the hosts you care about?

answer.diagnosis: Ansible judged the desired state already true — its comparison passed. Either the state IS there (look again, right host? right path?) or the task describes something subtly different from what you meant (wrong path, wrong file, wrong service name).
answer.fix: Read the task args against reality: exact path, exact name. Run with --check --diff to see what it compares. A template task that's 'ok' means the RENDERED content matched — maybe your variable change didn't reach this host (ansible-inventory --host).
answer.lesson: 'ok' means 'already true', not 'done nothing forever'. When ok surprises you, your model of the target is wrong somewhere specific.

answer.diagnosis: It changed... somewhere else. Wrong host matched, delegation sent it elsewhere, or you're checking a different box than Ansible touched.
answer.fix: --list-hosts the play; check delegate_to on the task; on the target, stat the file — timestamps don't lie.
answer.lesson: Verify on the machine, not in the recap. The recap is Ansible's opinion; stat is the courtroom evidence.

answer.diagnosis: A when: condition evaluated false for those hosts (or a tag filter excluded it).
answer.fix: Run with -vvv to see the skip reason; debug: the variables in the when: expression for that host; check --tags/--skip-tags on your command line.
answer.lesson: skipped is a silent 'no'. Conditions depending on facts need gather_facts on.

trees.title: A service won't start
trees.symptom: systemctl start fails, or the unit dies immediately.

start.q: Run systemctl status <unit> --no-pager -l. What does it show?

options.label: active but the thing doesn't work

logs.q: journalctl -u <unit> -b --no-pager | tail -50 — what's the actual complaint?

answer.diagnosis: The daemon rejected its own config.
answer.fix: Most daemons have a validator: sshd -t, httpd -t, nginx -t, named-checkconf, visudo -c. Run it, fix the named line, restart.
answer.lesson: Learn each daemon's -t flag. Validate BEFORE restart, every time — that's the pre-flight habit.

perm.q: Permission denied — is it filesystem or SELinux? Run: ausearch -m AVC -ts recent

answer.diagnosis: SELinux blocked it — mislabeled files or a boolean.
answer.fix: Files moved recently? restorecon -Rv <path>. Non-standard port/path? semanage port/fcontext. Service-to-network? getsebool -a | grep <svc>.
answer.lesson: mv preserves the old label; cp inherits the destination's. That asymmetry causes half of all AVCs.

answer.diagnosis: Classic ownership/mode problem on config, cert, socket, or state directory.
answer.fix: stat each path in the error; compare owner/mode to a working box or the package default (rpm -V <pkg> flags drift).
answer.lesson: rpm -V is your drift detector — it knows what the vendor shipped.

answer.diagnosis: Another process holds the port.
answer.fix: ss -tulpn | grep :<port>; kill the squatter properly (systemctl stop) or re-port one of them. Non-standard port + SELinux? semanage port -a -t <type> -p tcp <port>.
answer.lesson: On SELinux boxes a NEW port needs a policy entry too — bind failure isn't always a squatter.

answer.diagnosis: A file, mount, or dependency unit the service needs isn't there.
answer.fix: Read the unit: systemctl cat <unit> — check After=/Requires= and paths. findmnt the expected mounts; dnf provides the missing binary.
answer.lesson: systemctl cat shows the whole truth including drop-ins — read the unit before theorizing.

answer.diagnosis: The service starts and dies repeatedly; systemd's Restart= policy is looping it.
answer.fix: journalctl -u <unit> -b — find the FIRST failure of the loop, not the latest. systemctl reset-failed <unit> after fixing to clear rate-limiting.
answer.lesson: In a crash loop, scroll UP. The first death has the honest error; the rest are echoes.

answer.diagnosis: Unit name wrong or package not installed — or you edited a unit and forgot daemon-reload.
answer.fix: systemctl list-unit-files | grep -i <name>; dnf provides '*/<name>.service'; after any unit edit: systemctl daemon-reload.
answer.lesson: Unit names are exact. httpd on RHEL, apache2 on Debian — cross-distro memory betrays you here.

answer.diagnosis: Process is up but unreachable — port, bind address, or firewall.
answer.fix: ss -tulpn | grep <svc> — listening on 127.0.0.1 when clients are remote? Then firewall-cmd --list-all — is the port open? Then the client path (routing, DNS).
answer.lesson: Work outward: process → socket → firewall → network. One layer at a time, prove each.

trees.title: Disk full (or filling fast)
trees.symptom: No space left on device; df shows a filesystem at or near 100%.

options.label: df says full but du can't find it

answer.diagnosis: Runaway logs or journal growth — the most common fill.
answer.fix: du -xh /var | sort -rh | head -20. Journal too big? journalctl --disk-usage, then journalctl --vacuum-size=500M. A single service spamming? Fix its problem, then logrotate. Then set SystemMaxUse= in journald.conf so it can't recur.
answer.lesson: Don't just delete — cap. A cleanup without a cap is an appointment to do it again.

answer.diagnosis: Root filling is urgent — many services wedge at 100%.
answer.fix: du -xh / | sort -rh | head -20 (the -x matters — don't count other mounts). Usual suspects: /var on the root fs, crash dumps in /var/crash, old kernels. If LVM has VFree: lvextend -r the root LV.
answer.lesson: The -x flag keeps du honest across mounts. Without it you'll 'find' usage that lives on another filesystem.

answer.diagnosis: User data or scratch files — build artifacts, dumps, forgotten archives.
answer.fix: du -xh <mount> | sort -rh | head; find <mount> -size +500M -mtime +30 to list old big files. LIST first, decide with the owner, then remove.
answer.lesson: On multi-user boxes, deleting user files without asking is how trust dies. List, ask, then act.

answer.diagnosis: A deleted file is still held open — space stays claimed until the holding process lets go.
answer.fix: lsof +L1 — find processes holding deleted files; restart those services (systemctl restart). Space returns instantly.
answer.lesson: rm removes the name, not the file. The file dies when its last file handle closes — greybeard exam question.

trees.title: Can't SSH into a box
trees.symptom: Your own SSH to a server fails or times out (console access assumed).

start.q: What does ssh -v <host> show at the failure point?

answer.diagnosis: Packets aren't arriving — network path or a DROP firewall rule.
answer.fix: ping it; check the route/VLAN; from console: firewall-cmd --list-services includes ssh?; nmcli device status.
answer.lesson: Timeout = black hole (DROP or no path). Refused = alive but door shut. Different diseases, read the symptom precisely.

answer.diagnosis: Host is alive; nothing is listening on that port (sshd down or moved).
answer.fix: Console: systemctl status sshd; ss -tlnp | grep sshd. Non-standard port? Check sshd_config Port — and remember SELinux needs semanage port for a custom SSH port.
answer.lesson: Refused is GOOD news — the box is up and telling you exactly which layer to fix.

answer.diagnosis: sshd rejected the credentials.
answer.fix: Console: tail /var/log/secure while retrying — sshd states the reason (bad ownership on .ssh, no matching key, user not allowed). Check AllowUsers/AllowGroups in sshd_config; restorecon -Rv ~/.ssh.
answer.lesson: /var/log/secure is sshd's confession log. One retry while tailing beats an hour of guessing.

answer.diagnosis: Auth succeeded but the session dies: broken shell, full disk, or a hostile ForceCommand/profile.
answer.fix: Console: getent passwd <user> — valid shell? df -h — full filesystem? Check /etc/nologin existence; try ssh <host> 'echo ok' (no PTY) to isolate.
answer.lesson: Login-then-boot means PAM/shell/profile territory, not sshd proper. The handshake worked; the house is broken.
